pr_body:
The insecure flag now disables TLS verification on https requests

Fixes #2622
pr_comments: I don't really have a strong opinion on what the final UX should be, but the primary use-case I was trying to solve for is end-users who have (corp) proxies that are running with untrusted server certs, and for whatever reason, wiring those root certs into the system to get Go to trust it is non-trivial.  It's certainly not universal, but I thought our `--insecure` flag was equivalent to curl's, and was surprised that it downgraded the scheme from https -> http.  Initially this PR just "fixed that" but it was pointed out that some developers are running their own registries locally and are relying on that flag to run over http, so we most likely need two flags/settings to satisfy these different use-cases.
Going to close this given its age, however we'd want to support looking at the URL's protocol (e.g. `https` or` http`), with a flag for overriding security checks (e.g. skipping tls verification)

review_comments:
Also, doesn't this break the current behavior? If I'm used to this flag only changing `https` to `http` and now it does not do that, and instead skips TLS verification without rewriting the scheme, that is not the behavior I would expect. I would want it to push to the http endpoint or none at all, not skip TLS verification.

If that is not what is happening, my bad, but maybe we need to rethink the docs here. If it is what is happening, then: 

I'd like to preempt any "Insecure is insecure" counterpoints with: "This is a breaking change." and propose we simply update the `-insecure` flag with more thought. See proposal in comment below.

What happens if I set this _and_ `-insecure`? Is it a nop, an error? It's confusing to have these two flags. It's always confusing to have flags that get canceled out, silently, by another.

I would also be unfortunate to have the two flags, when they could be one, and without breaking the existing behavior that `-insecure` has today.

A (very serious) proposal:

Change the flag to be  _set_ (or simply present), like: `-insecure[="https-only" | "http-only" | "skip-verify"]`. The rules are:

- If present but without a value (e.g. `-insecure`) it defaults to http-only, which is the behavior today.
- If present and set, do what the value says
- If not present, default to `https-only`

The values mean:

- `https-only`: Use HTTPS, always verify TLS
- `skip-verify`: Use HTTPS, but skip TLS verification
- `http-only`: Use HTTP, only. There is no TLS to skip or verify.

> NOTE: The https-only value is there for completeness and should be allowed as a value even though it could be "set" but not using the flag at all.

This is not the most ideal situation to be in, I know. However, the flag was unfortunately introduced to mean something other that "skip TLS verification", so here we are.

In conclusion, the above proposal allows us to maintain the current behavior/meaning of the `-insecure` flag, and allows us to avoid introducing an admittedly ambiguous and confusing `-http` flag.

We should look at the scheme in the url in the arg for this instead of a new flag.

If `--insecure` is provided and no scheme: use http
If `--insecure` is provided and the `https://` scheme is in the arg, use https

@jmorganca I disagree that what you describe should be the behavior. That is surprising behavior. I've never seen a type of insecure flag mean "downgrade the insecurity by 1 unit from whatever it is now".

Being more explicit would be easier to grok. "When you say insecure, exactly how insecure?" is more like what one might expect to be answering when using such a flag.

Also, if there exists a URL already, then just use the scheme in the URL. Why even have the insecure flag? We could introduce a `-skip-verify` flag, but then we should probably think through the behavior when it is combined with a url that is http only. I would assume it fails and says "remove flag to proceed" in so many words.
